name: Why inference routing matters for agentic workloads
use_case:
Scenario 1 comes from building side projects on SI — every so often a model isn't reachable(ex: gemma incident), and I end up writing failover by hand. 
Scenario 2 came out of today's sales kickoff: if we're telling customers to eval and adopt newer models,
 the obvious next question is how they cut over without interrupting live traffic.
pain_value:
Pain points:

Models go down in production, engineers manually write failover logic
Switching to newer models risks breaking live traffic

Value prop:

Automatic failover with a one-line config change — no code rewrite
Live model switching in ~2s — zero deploys, zero downtime, zero client changes
Fully auditable via server-side headers, not black-box magic
brief:
Scenario 1- Failover: A 3-step agent (retrieve → summarize → extract) serves the same request in two lanes while the primary endpoint starts failing. Identical agent code — the only difference is one tuple in config: `(PRIMARY,)` vs `(PRIMARY, ALT)`. The single-endpoint lane burns its retries and dies. The routed lane fails over and finishes.

Each lane shows what the user sees (a chat — the routed user never learns a failover happened) next to what ops sees (the decision log, full of 429s and routing decisions), with a to-scale request timeline below. Faults come from a local proxy: deterministic, same outcome every run, and says nothing about any provider's real limits.

Scenario 2 - Adoption: This one drives the real Inference Router. Two lanes serve the same request stream: one model hard-coded, one calling `router:agent-demo-router`. Mid-stream we reorder the router's ranking via PUT /v2/gen-ai/models/routers/{id}(observed propagation ~2s) and every later response is served by the new model. Zero client changes, zero deploys, zero failed requests.

The proof is in the responses: the model field is written server-side, and every response carries x-model-router-selected-route showing the router — not the client — picked it.

name: From ticket to PR - Coding Agent
use_case: Enhance a software engineering team with Agents. Agents pick up work automatically from Jira tickets and work autonomously on the GIthub Repository by creating PRs. Independent agents also perform QA on the Pull Requests and provide their feedback. By the time a human reviews an issue, a PR is already in place and a full review of it has been done, massively speeding up the traditional software development process.
pain_value: Every codebase has a backlog of issues which sit there for weeks and take the focus from more interesting work. In this demo, we show can MARS agents can be invoked directly from Jira tickets to fix issues on a Github repository and open PRs. In addition, independent agents review and validate the PRs - Approving or Rejecting them and leaving their feedback. By the time a human engineer steps in, a review is open and already reviewed, massively speeding up the process of fixing these issues.
brief: Shows a simluated Jira board. You pick an issue and click "launch agent". An agent works on the issue and opens a PR against the Github repo. That triggers another agent that reviews the PR and either Approves or Rejects it and posts their feedback.

name: Ops Runbook Agent (Incident Copilot)
use_case: Useful when the conversation is about cutting mean time to resolve, standardizing incident response, or showing how on-call teams can get a diagnosis and draft plan before the war room fills. Strong fit for discovery and POC calls with SRE, Platform, and DevOps leaders who own reliability, as well as short executive walkthroughs where the story is “alert in → investigation and runbook out, with humans still approving production changes.”
products:
DigitalOcean Harness Runtime (MARS) :  for isolated agent sessions, 
Serverless Inference for model reasoning without a GPU fleet, 
Action Gateway for human approval of production changes, 
 App Platform as the console hosting the live experience.
pain_value: Most incidents still burn the first ten minutes on tribal knowledge — who owns the runbook, which dashboard to open, and which deploy likely caused the outage. This demo shows agents investigating inside isolated Harness sessions, correlating metrics, logs, and deploys, then drafting a gated runbook and postmortem while humans still own every production change. The value is faster MTTR with bounded autonomy: speed without giving the agent unconstrained write access.
brief: A pager-style alert lands on an incident board. One click dispatches triage and runbook agents into fresh Harness Runtime sandboxes. Agents reason through Gradient Serverless Inference, stream tool calls live in the console, and return a working diagnosis, approval-gated mitigation steps, a customer-ready status note, and a postmortem draft. Guardrails deny destructive actions such as rm -rf. The recommended path is INC-104 (SEV-1 canary); INC-105 demonstrates policy denial; offline replay is available when the network or MARS path is unreliable

name: Database Change Tracker

pain_value: App teams and administrators often ask "what changed" when issues arise. This involves looking in various places and querying system tables in the database, likely requiring several custom queries to look for different types of changes. This would allow anyone to ask semantic questions and get a comprehensive list of changes.
brief: Ask questions to the agent and show a before and after when changes are made. Either a doc or screen recording.

name: Weaviate Data Ingestion
use_case: Automate the creation and ingestion of a Weaviate database from a source (file or Postgres table)
pain_value: Being a new technology, vector databases are a relative unknown as to how to build them out correctly. App team want to deploy their applications quickly, and trying to understand how to build a schema in a vector database can be challenging. This concept would analyze the current structure of the source data and map that to Weaviate and load the data.

name: Sandboxed Application Security Agent
use_case: Application security scanning securely in a sandbox.
pain_value: MARS runs every security scan in its own disposable microVM, so untrusted code can be tested without putting your infrastructure at risk. Each scan gets a hardware-isolated sandbox on Managed Agents Environments, is destroyed the moment it finishes, and leaves nothing behind to clean up, patch, or worry about. You get stronger isolation and lower cost, because you pay only for the seconds each scan runs.
brief: A sandboxed environment to test github repos and specifically applications for security vulnerabilities.
